question.problem:
Which of the following equalities are true given that
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,-1\le y\le 1\}.$

I. ${∬}_{D}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$

II. ${∬}_{D}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$

III. ${∬}_{D}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y$
question.worked_solution:
We notice that:

- the limits for the variable $x$ are from $0$ to $2$, and

- the limits for the variable $y$ are from $-1$ to $1.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the region of integration is rectangular, we can simply swap the order of integration. This gives

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{x-1}{y+2}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x.
$$

So, the correct answer is "II only".
